label: rem:h3-markov-wenzl-weights-context
title: Scope, Borromean corollary, chirality, and notation for the $H_3$ Wenzl weights
html:
Scope — which trace, in which channel

This proposition concerns the Jones / Temperley–Lieb normalisation of the \mathrm{H}_3(q) Markov trace — the trace at Ocneanu parameter z = q^3/(q^2+1) whose value on a braid closure is the Jones polynomial. Its defining feature is y_{(1^3)} \equiv 0: the Temperley–Lieb quotient annihilates the three-row partition.

Both the mass and binding channels use this trace uniformly across the framework, and the parameter is forced by the fibre decomposition: the eigenbasis decomposition for the Feynman amplitude imposes the row cap \ell(\lambda) \leq 2 inside the index set of V^{\otimes n} \cong \bigoplus V_\lambda \otimes S_\lambda, giving y_{(1^3)} = 0, and the Markov-trace selection theorem then makes z = q^3/(q^2+1) the unique faithful normalised Markov trace (entering through the Borromean Markov trace and the dressing factor F_{\mathrm{Bor}} into the nucleon mass). Independently, the Ocneanu parameter determines the fibre rank through z \cdot [N]_q = q^{N-1} q = q^N, which is injective in N for q > 1 and yields the integer rank N = 2 at z = q^3/(q^2+1). Note also the generator distinction in primitive Markov-trace axioms (M1–M4) and Categorical mass as Markov trace: the Temperley–Lieb loop reciprocal 1/\delta = 1/[2]_q evaluates the Temperley–Lieb generator e_i = q - \sigma_i, whereas under \sigma-stabilisation \mathrm{tr}_M(e_i) = q - z = 1/[2]_q gives z = q^3/(q^2+1). At q = 1 the weights reduce to (\tfrac12,\tfrac14,0), and at q_0 they evaluate to (0.5054,\,0.2473,\,0).

What writhe 0 does and does not buy. For \beta \in B_3 with writhe 0 and \pi(\beta) = \mathrm{id} both one-dimensional characters equal 1, so by the corollary below the trace depends on the weights only through y_{(2,1)}: the split between y_{(3)} and y_{(1^3)} is invisible, because normalisation \sum_\lambda y_\lambda d_\lambda = 1 already pins y_{(3)} + y_{(1^3)} = 1 - 2y_{(2,1)}. This is why the chirality asymmetry between (3) and (1^3) is unobservable on such braids. It does not make \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta) independent of the Markov parameter z: two normalised Markov traces \mathrm{tr}_M, \mathrm{tr}'_M with weights y, y' agree on such a braid precisely when y_{(2,1)} = y'_{(2,1)} or \chi^{(2,1)}(\beta) = 2, and on \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} (\chi^{(2,1)}(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) = 2 - 3h^4 - h^6 \neq 2 for h \neq 0),

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) - \mathrm{tr}'_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}})
  \;=\;
  \bigl(y_{(2,1)} - y'_{(2,1)}\bigr)\bigl(-3h^4 - h^6\bigr).

Immediate corollary — the Borromean closed form in one line

For any writhe-0 braid \beta \in B_3 with \pi(\beta) = \mathrm{id} \in S_3:

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta)
  \;=\;
  1 + \frac{\chi^{(2,1)}(\beta) - 2}{[2]_q^{2}}.

The entire h-dependence of such traces is carried by the single standard-channel character; the Borromean closed form is this identity evaluated at \chi^{(2,1)}(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) = 2 - 3h^4 - h^6.

Non-uniformity of the weights — chirality of the Jones trace

A bar-involution argument would suggest y_{(3)} = y_{(1^3)} (the transpose pair). It fails: the transpose symmetry \lambda \leftrightarrow \lambda^T is induced by the sign-twist automorphism \sigma_i \mapsto -q\,\sigma_i^{-1}, and the Jones-normalised Markov trace is not invariant under this automorphism — it is chiral, weighting the \sigma- and \sigma^{-1}-eigenchannels asymmetrically. The extreme expression of this asymmetry is y_{(1^3)} \equiv 0 against y_{(3)}(1) = 1/2.

At q = 1 the trace reduces to the cycle-counting trace \mathrm{tr}_M(w) = 2^{\,c(w) - n} on \mathbb{C}[S_3] (c(w) = number of cycles), and Schur orthogonality reproduces (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, 0) directly.

Notation note — y_\lambda, \mu_\lambda, \chi^\lambda, w_\lambda are distinct

Four \lambda-indexed scalars appear in the Hecke-algebra blocks of this paper. They are easy to conflate by symbol similarity but encode independent data:

  • y_\lambda(q) — Wenzl/Markov coefficient: appears in \mathrm{tr}_M = \sum_\lambda y_\lambda \cdot \chi^\lambda, normalised by \sum_\lambda y_\lambda \, d_\lambda = 1. This proposition gives the Jones/Temperley–Lieb values at z = q^3/(q^2+1), for which y_{(1^3)} \equiv 0.
  • \chi^\lambda(g) — character: trace of the V_\lambda-representation on a specific element g (e.g. a braid).
  • \mu_\lambda(q) — q-Laplacian eigenvalue on V_\lambda (Peter--Weyl decomposition of the q-heat kernel (archimedean)): the heat-kernel decay rate, not a Markov-trace ingredient.
  • w_\lambda(q) = [n]_q! / H_q(\lambda)^2 — Plancherel measure (The symmetric point loses resolution, not spectrum): normalised by \sum_\lambda w_\lambda(1) = 1 at q = 1 only — the q-deformed sum \sum_\lambda w_\lambda(q) is not 1 (0.987 at n = 3, 1.051 at n = 8); at q = 1 it is non-uniform in a different pattern (\tfrac16, \tfrac23, \tfrac16 for n = 3) from the Wenzl weights of this proposition (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, 0).

Significance for the Borromean derivation

The 1/4 factor in h^4(\mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}})) = (-3) \cdot (1/4) = -3/4 is y_{(2,1)}(q = 1) = 1/[2]_q^2|_{q=1} from this proposition — and the identity y_{(2,1)}(q) = 1/[2]_q^2 holds exactly for all q, not only at the symmetric point. The Borromean h^4 separation into character coefficient \times Markov normalisation is therefore an exact structural fact, with the (h^2 + 4) denominator of the closed form being precisely [2]_q^2 = 1/y_{(2,1)}(q).

The q = 1 weights (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, 0) are not uniform, since the Jones trace is not sign-twist invariant. They are verified three ways: Schur orthogonality on the q = 1 cycle-counting trace, the exact q-dependent closed forms above, and canonical reproduction of the Borromean closed form at 30 digits.
